title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma 2 Foundations of Mindfulness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of mindfulness as a practice that allows us to direct our attention and influence what we're aware of, much like a spotlight shining on different aspects of experience. By cultivating mindfulness, we can develop a greater understanding and appreciation for reality, including our own bodies and attitudes towards them, in order to guide wholesome states in body and mind. This practice is meant to be repeated and refined over time, rather than just memorized or studied once, in order to establish a life of purity and bring happiness to oneself and others.

sentences.text: Here are a few paragraphs from the sutra that describes the Buddha's death, called the parinirvana, final nirvana.
The Buddha is speaking, lying down between some trees.
The monks are gathered, and nuns, and lay people too, people from far and wide, I guess.
The Buddha uses this time to teach, and this isn't quite the end.
There are several chapters, but towards the end he uses this time to teach what he'd already been teaching for 45 years.
He said:

*Oh monks and nuns, I say to you that these teachings of which I have direct knowledge, and which have been made known to you, these you should thoroughly learn, cultivate, develop, and frequently practice, that the life of purity may be established and may long endure, for the welfare and happiness of the multitude, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, well-being, and happiness of gods and humans.

And what, oh monks and nuns, are these teachings?* [unclear: "You know that you should do all this with."] *They are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four constituents of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

These are the teachings of which I have direct knowledge, which I have made known to you, and which you should thoroughly learn, cultivate, develop, and frequently practice, so that the life of purity may be established and may long endure, for the welfare and happiness of the multitude, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, well-being, and happiness of gods and humans.*
*Then the Blessed One said to the monks and nuns, I exhort you, all compound things are subject to vanish.
Strive with earnestness.
The time of the Tathagata's parinirvana is near.
Soon the Tathagata will pass utterly away.*
*And having spoken these words, the Happy One, the Great Master, spoke again, saying in verse, My ears are now full ripe, the lifespan left is short.
Departing, I go hence from you, relying on myself alone.
Be earnest then, O monks and nuns.
Be mindful and pure of virtue.
With firm resolve, guard your mind.
Who so untiringly pursues the Dharma and the discipline, shall go beyond the rounds of births and make an end of suffering.*
This is an excerpt of the Parinirvana Sutra, so heavy-duty stuff.
What's interesting is that he didn't have some new, secret, special teaching for the very end.
He returned to things that he had been teaching, and these monks and nuns had been studying and working with for many years.
So there's this sense of keeping going, simple practice, over and over and over again.
Let me read you that list of verbs, so we know what our charge is here.
According to this sutra, you should learn, thoroughly learn, cultivate, develop, and frequently practice.
That's the action items on the agenda.
Thoroughly learn, cultivate, develop, and frequently practice.
It's not a one-time thing: frequently practice.
Then he gives a purpose to this, like why would you do all this?

The purpose is so that the life of purity may be established and long endure, and so that the welfare and happiness of the multitude, out of compassion for the world, so it's going to help everybody, the whole world, for the benefit, wellbeing, and happiness of gods and humans.
He gives a bunch of lists, a list of lists.
This is the list of lists that I'm on about lately.
So you're stuck with it for a while.
Here's a handout that you want to be looking at.
I thought we'd get started tonight.
We had a great long talk a couple weeks ago, and we didn't get to the list.
Oh, I have one of those back.
Sorry, I need the list too.
This handout that I gave you is 37 items long, arranged in seven lists.
In the second paragraph of the sutra, that's what he's referring to.
I'm trying to make enough, huh?
Sorry.
I'll give you mine.
You can look on.
I've arranged them a little bit with a little introductory verse and a closing verse as a ceremony we can do, and we did do together once.
I've been really enjoying doing the ceremony in my home practice, and I recommend it.
One thing about these teachings from early Buddhism is that they can seem a little dry at first, right?
These lists, I just gave you this list, and now you're trying to take it in.

There's a lot of repeated words, there's a lot of unfamiliar words, and so it's wonderful to find ways to bring these lists and teachings to life so that we really learn them and bring them into our bodies.
So I've been chanting this and bowing with each of these 37 items in the morning at home.

I thought I'd give you just a little more background on the whole list, and we'd start talking about the first set tonight, which we've talked about before, but I have some new ways of thinking about them that might be helpful.
In this sutra, the Buddha listed these seven lists, this list of seven, which later came to be called, in Mahayana Buddhism, the Bodhi Pakshika Dharma.
Bodhi means awakening.
Pakshika means things that relate to something.
And Dharma has a really wonderful double meaning.
It's going to show up several times in the title, and it'll show up several times in the list, too.
In English, the two meanings are usually distinguished in writing with a capital D and a lowercase d, but I don't think they have capitalization in Sanskrit, so I think that's an English convention.
Must be some English guy in Sri Lanka invented that, Rhys Davids or somebody.
So Big D Dharma is the Buddha's teaching, the teachings of the Buddha.
In a way, the first meaning is things that relate to the Buddha's teaching and awakening, so that makes sense.
But Little D Dharma means experience, experience itself.
They had a whole complicated system in early Buddhism of evaluating experience.
They meditated so darn much that they started to distinguish very fine granularity in experience, and they created a whole taxonomy of experiences that you can have.
These are dharmas, like an atom of experience, the smallest unit of experience you can have.
So that's interesting, that this word dharma means Buddha's teachings that lead to liberation, and at the same time means experience itself.
So what's implied there?

Well, lots of things, and you should think about it yourself, but one possibility is it's suggesting that the Buddha's teachings are not something new that is put on top of experience, not some external organizing principle or description or something like that, but rather a way of looking at experience itself that's more skillful, or leads to more happiness, or leads to complete freedom from suffering, depending on how you look at it.
So this list has both of those elements.
It's rooted in experience.
These are not just things to memorize and try to remember and put post-its on your fridge.
Well, you could do that.
They're rooted in the experience of our living itself, ways of re-imagining and re-understanding and re-investigating experience itself.
Another thing I remembered was that when I was in college I was studying biology, mostly botany, which is the study of plants.
There's an awful lot of plants in North America, and other parts of the world are even more diverse.
I found it really baffling.
I couldn't remember the names of the plants until I took what they call systematics in botany, which is learning an organizing principle.
You learn plant families, and the plant families have characteristics, and the families are divided, there's different divisions and orders and stuff.
It was the weirdest thing.
Suddenly it all came together.
I didn't know every plant in North America, but suddenly I had something to hang my hat on.
Suddenly it was significantly easier to understand, much, much easier to learn new plants, with something to fit them into.

So last year when I ran into a book on this list of lists by Chan Master Sheng Yen, here's the book, I thought, wow, there's a way of organizing all these early Buddhist teachings, taught to us by a Chinese Zen master.
So there's a very direct connection to our way of practice, and to earlier Buddhism.
It also turns out this list of lists is studied extensively by Theravadan practitioners and scholars.
There's a great long, long book about this list by Thanissaro Bhikkhu, who was sitting right here this last weekend.
That's surprising.
Hiya, John.
Unfortunately we weren't here.
Was anybody there?
No, we were there.
Maybe next time.
And he has a great long list with lots of excerpts from the Pali Canon.
So I thought this is a list that transcends different Buddhisms, because there's really not just one, there are many Buddhisms.
It can provide us with a topology of applied practice.
As I went on and on about a couple weeks ago, and you can listen for it on the website if you want to, we can hold this with a certain spirit, though.
It would be easier for us to turn this long list into a huge to-do list, a really huge to-do list, which we will never quite do right, always failing and falling down.
So we're coming into this with a spirit from our Zen practice, a spirit of stability, a spirit of completeness in this moment.
We're both fine, we're already fine.
We just need to relax into being fine, goodness gracious.
And we could use a little improvement, and we could pay a heck of a lot more attention to our experience.
So I thought it would be useful.
The first section of the Bodhipakshika Dharma is the four foundations of mindfulness.
This word, mindfulness, is in the air a lot lately.
It's being applied outside of Buddhism, and it's a construct that's used in many different branches of Buddhism.
The word mindfulness itself shows up again and again in the other lists.
So the first list is about mindfulness, and then mindfulness is also in the other lists.
Actually, just this morning I was here teaching a secular form of mindfulness, and it really seems to help people a lot.
There were 20 people in the room, most of whom had never meditated before, studying mindfulness.
It seemed to really be helpful to them.
So, four foundations of mindfulness.
This comes straight from an early Buddhist text called the Mindfulness Sutra, the Satipatthana Sutta.
These different secular trainings are basically based on this sutra, as is this list.
So the importance of this first list is really hard to underestimate.
It's really huge.
Sitting there with a couple of words on a piece of paper, it doesn't look like much, but it's quite a huge and important thing.
The Pali word that's translated as mindfulness is Sati.
Pali is the language in which they first wrote down Buddhist teachings, in southern India and Sri Lanka.
There's an analogous word in Sanskrit, which is something like smriti.
So mindfulness is an English word, right?
You wonder what they really meant.
What did the Buddha mean?
There are these layers.
The number one meaning for this word Sati is remembering, to remember.
So it's a process, it's a verb, not really a state.
The word mindful gets used both ways, mindful, mindfulness.
It's used in English as a verb and as a noun, right?
People could say, you should be mindful, or he wasn't very mindful.
So that's an adjective, too.
It's used in different ways.
But in the traditional sense, the question is mindful of what?
Remembering what?
What are you mindful of?
Remembering is great, but you know what you're remembering.
This first list of four foundations provides four areas of remembering, and we could take each one of these up and study them for quite a while, years probably.
Foundation is in the sense of something to stand on, like the foundation of a house.
Taking up one of these foundations of mindfulness is a process of choosing an area of our experience to be the foundation of our life while we're studying it.
So we take up each of these foundations as an area of study, study of experience, study of this process of remembering.
I'll get to how in a minute.
Thanissaro Bhikkhu has an interesting translation, a pretty free translation.
The words do mean something like foundation of mindfulness, but he translated it instead as frame of reference.
Frame of reference.
So each of these is a frame of reference or a foundation.
And one way I've been thinking about mindfulness, so we'll get back to the four foundations, is as a process, and what does that mean actually?
We have this consciousness and this thinking and we're aware of stuff, but what's actually happening?
Here's one possible way to think about that.
I've been using the analogy lately of a spotlight in the theater.
You've been in the theater, right, so they have a spotlight.
They can move it around and shine it on the stage.
Say it's a dark scene, and most of the stage can't be seen, and the spotlight is shining on one actor.
So all you can really see or be aware of is that one actor.
The spotlight is casting light, so the light is enabling awareness.
Awareness is one thing: you can be aware of something.
But then the spotlight can move around, right?
Deliberately maybe.
Maybe not so deliberately.
Things grab our attention, so that's attention.
Attention is this moving spotlight.
The spotlight is creating light, it creates awareness, so there's attention and awareness.
And then mindfulness is this.
You're sitting in this dark theater, engrossed in the show of your life.
The spotlight's moving around.
Different things are popping into your consciousness and you're like, whoa, seems a little bit out of control, right?
Then you remember that you're actually sitting on a stool right in front of the spotlight with your hands on the handles of the thing.
You forgot that you can actually move the spotlight.
So mindfulness is the remembering that you can actually direct attention and have some influence over what you're aware of.
Do you like that metaphor?
That's really helping me to think about this this way.
We don't have complete control of our spotlight, right?
Things happen from the outside.
External events that grab our attention shift the spotlight over there.
It just happened.
And then there are internal events that grab the spotlight and move it around, right?
A terrible memory or worry about the future.
This moves the spotlight, sometimes turning the spotlight right onto our self a certain way.
So that's awareness, attention and mindfulness.
Then one last word to have some vocabulary to think about consciousness: concentration.
Concentration is holding that spotlight steadily, so that we're holding attention on one something.
So there's some consistency to awareness and some stability.
And usually we're able to calm down a little bit.
And perfect timing.

One last aspect of this metaphor that's helpful is that you can not only direct your spotlight around the stage of your life and look at different things, have different things in awareness, but you can also focus the beam, right?
It can be really narrow, so you're just looking at one little teeny aspect of experience.
Or you can open it up wide.
the light shining on the whole stage, less bright, probably because it's spread out more.
But you can in some way see the whole of your life.
So mindfulness practice is working with this.
Remembering that it's possible, for one thing, because you forget that you're actually holding the spotlight.
You can't move it, right?
And like I say, it's not some kind of hardcore attentional control training: just do enough mindfulness training here and you'll never ever be distracted again.
But we have a lot more influence and freedom in this than maybe we think we do, just by virtue of the remembering, just by virtue of the remembering.
So that's a few metaphors about awareness, attention, mindfulness, and concentration.
Four key concepts.

This list of four foundations of mindfulness, the first of the Bodhipaksika Dharma, suggests four places we might want to shine our spotlight and see if we can hold the spotlight there steadily and investigate that aspect of our life.
It starts with the body.
That's why I said a few words during Zazen at the beginning about the body.
Zen is more or less explicit that the body is involved: we pay attention to posture.
Some other schools of Buddhism don't pay too much attention to posture.
But still, we come in here with our mind, right?
The thinking is motoring along, as it always is.
And we're thinking about how we are doing.
Are we doing a good job in our Zazen tonight?
Oh, not too good.
And we lose track of the actual experience of being embodied.
So the Buddha suggests start with the body, return to the body.
In a way this is really straightforward: actually notice sensations in the body, the felt experience of the body.
In the mindfulness sutra, there are some funny phrases.
It says that we should be mindful of the body in the body, the body in the body.
It's not like some outside agent looking at the body, like we're out here somewhere: "Oh, look at that body, wow."
But the body in the body, and Tanasaro translates that as the body in and of itself, in and of itself.
So sensations in the body, feelings in the body, and breath is included here.
The breathing is a process of the body, which we treasure in Zen as they do in all schools of Buddhism.
Because the breath is such a great support, isn't it?
It's always there, ready to remind you of what's happening now.
But the other thing that's included in mindfulness of the body, which is interesting, you wouldn't think this, is looking also at attitudes that spring from the body.
Pause for a minute and consider this question.
Do you like your body a little bit?
Maybe a few improvements are needed?
Is your body the exact right weight, for instance?
Height?
Curves all just right?
Is your hair okay? [unclear: "Saves us one thing."] There's enough left.
What's interesting about traditional Buddhism is the way they expressed this investigation of attitude about the body: they talked a lot about the impurity of the body.
They must have had some theory in medieval India about the body as a pure thing that the Buddha was working with.
Because it goes on and on about the impurity of the body, and I don't think we need that wording exactly.
It's super easy for us to be convinced that our body is just a mess, right?
Impure.
I think for us it's to be really aware of our attitude and understanding of the body, and can we align that attitude and understanding with reality and with appreciation.
Reality and appreciation.
Because this is the only body we get, right?
So we need to take care of it.
It's our only body.
Our only way of being alive.
Our only vehicle of practice and love and joy.
And there are a variety of practices we can do to study the body throughout our culture.
In a way, it's so interesting, we do have a kind of cult of the body.
We have all these gyms and yoga classes and martial arts and things.
And yet there's also a certain way that even through all these disciplines and good, healthy things we try to do, long hikes, there's a way that we hold the body at arm's length, too.
Like, "I am taking my body to the gym to take care of it."
So who am I?
Where is the body?
This practice of the foundation of mindfulness of the body is more of a deep entering into the body from the inside of the body.
How do we hold the body?
How do we feel about the body?
How do we care for the body?
One way to look at it, and there are many different ways to study this, one possible way, is to look at it from the point of view of the three poisons, right?
Sometimes they say greed, hatred and ignorance.
You could say desire, anger and confusion, if you want.
So notice, how does desire arise in relationship to the body?
Is there a wanting the body to be different?
Is there a wanting the body to change?
Or is there a wanting the body to not change?
Like, I thought I would get to show off my reading glasses tonight, but I forgot them.
Fortunately the lectern is far enough away.
All of a sudden I need reading glasses, and I didn't sign up for that.
So there's desire, right?
There's greed that manifests in our attitudes in the body.
And we can work with that.
We can recognize that.
We can turn to that.
Practice with it.
Mindfulness, right?
Bringing awareness back.
Ah, there's greed in my study of mindfulness of the body.
We can be angry at the body, right?
When it lets us down, when it gets sick, when it fails.
When it's not quite doing what we want it to do.
And then we can be confused about the nature of the body.
So there are all three poisons right there, and you can use lots of different frames to study the body.
I had planned to talk about the other four foundations, but maybe that's enough.
I'm really trying to learn how to give shorter talks.
I'm not very good at it.
So let's consider this first foundation of mindfulness these next weeks, having this little bit of framing that this is the beginning of a bigger process.
What's neat as we study these other lists as well is that they work together in interesting ways.
That's part of why I was really happy about this list of lists being a traditional thing.
Most of these I studied separately.
They tend to pop up independently, and you study them and you put them down and forget about them.
What's been really interesting, thinking about them together, is the ways that they support each other.
The second set of four, maybe I'll just say a few words about the second set of four, because they work beautifully with the first four.
The four proper exertions.
And this is another experiential, moment-by-moment thing that we can talk a lot more about later.
Guarding against unwholesome states, and you can add "not yet."
I shortened these a little for chanting, so the full thing is guarding against unwholesome states that have not yet arisen.
So what can we do to reduce the arising of things that are difficult, unwholesome, unhealthy, causing suffering?
What can we do to guard against the arising of those unwholesome states?
But then the Buddha was so realistic, he's like, okay, but then they come anyway.
So the second point he makes is abandoning unwholesome states once they have arisen.
You guard against them, some come anyway, so then you work on releasing from those.
And then he says, cultivating wholesome states not yet arisen.
So how do we set up our life and our schedule and our work and our eating and our everything to make it more possible for wholesome states to arise?
Whatever those may be, and we'll investigate that later.
Things that feel deeply right, maybe is one way to say it.
Things that increase awareness, increase lasting joy and contentment.
And then he says, maintaining wholesome states once they have arisen.
So how do we keep those things?
What's interesting about this teaching is that it seems, on the face of it, to fly in the face of "just accept everything."
This is a fairly manipulative instruction, right?
Set up your life to reduce this and increase that.
So there is actually discernment and manipulation in Buddhist practice.
It's just a question of how we do it.
What's truly skillful and how we work with the mind.
And one thing that I've been really using, so that we can use all this frame to study the body, right?
How do we guard against unwholesome states arising in the body and so on?
And we can use this second set of four with all kinds of stuff, too.
I've been really interested in this in regard to self-talk.
What are the ways that we talk to ourselves about what's happening that cultivate wholesome or unwholesome states?
I see some heads nodding, you know this?
We actually have some influence over our thinking, or at least how we regard and feed our thinking.
So these teachings are really helpful.
So maybe that's enough for tonight.
And this is what we'll study at the study retreat, which is I think two weekends from this coming one or something like that, or a week from this coming one?

Leslie gave them fresh plums.

But it was so beautiful, and they had really purified the body and mind somehow during this practice.
They were really glowing and very content.
And sore knees and [unclear: "knock back"] kind of stuff, of course.
I just wanted to mention that that went really well.
Bob and I are trying to think about how we could do more of that work, and how that will fit into Song of Life, who knows.
But somehow this vision came true.
So I just wanted to mention that since you didn't get to be there.
And we'll do other kinds of wilderness things too, I think, that are more accessible and closer to home as well.
And actually, I don't know what the ino has planned, but I can't be here next week.
So if you're around, Bob, I wonder if you could say a few words next week about what that whole experience was and what you guys did and tell the story.
Tell the story for that one there.

Wow.

Is that okay?

I just want to sit.
